payload.rationale: Observed: CDC reports 3,471 confirmed 2026 U.S. measles cases as of September 17, 2026 (updated Sept 18), with 39 outbreaks and 95% outbreak-associated. Reaching >6,000 requires ~2,530 additional cases in roughly the remaining 15 weeks of the year (plus any post-year reporting lag captured before settlement), i.e., about 170 cases/week sustained. The year-to-date average is ~94/week, and that average is inflated by the late-winter/spring seasonal peak; fall is historically a lower-transmission period, and even the sizable late-2025 outbreaks (Utah/Arizona, South Carolina) produced weekly national counts well below the required pace. The outbreak count (39) indicates ongoing multi-focal transmission and undervaccinated communities remain vulnerable, so a large new outbreak in a low-coverage community (analogous to West Texas in early 2025) is plausible but would need to be unusually explosive and start almost immediately. Rash-onset year assignment and CDC's confirmed-only reporting also cap late additions. Too low if: an already-seeded large outbreak in an undervaccinated community is accelerating now (no weekly trend supplied), reporting backlogs release a large batch, or holiday-season travel seeds several simultaneous outbreaks that show up before settlement. Too high if: seasonal decline holds and weekly counts drift toward 50–80, making even 5,000 unreachable. Net: a roughly 1.8x acceleration over the annual average during the off-season is a tail scenario, so ~8%.
limitations: No weekly incidence series or trend data supplied; assessment of current growth rate is inferred from cumulative totals and seasonal priors.
CDC counts are provisional and revised; timing of the settlement snapshot relative to year-end reporting lag is uncertain.
Seasonality assumption drawn from historical U.S. patterns (2019, 2025) may not hold if a large undervaccinated-community outbreak is underway.
Single-source packet; no independent verification of the Sept 17 figure.
